::: {.callout-warning}
## Before you connect anything

An analog input pin tolerates $0$ to $V_\mathrm{io}$ and nothing else — 3.3 V
on most supported boards, 5 V on the Renesas ones. There is no protection
worth relying on. Measure every source with the DMM **before** it touches a
pin, check the board's own logic voltage with `arduino-io info`, and never
assume a bench supply is where you left it.

On a Portenta H7, pins A0–A3 read up to 3.3 V through on-board dividers, so
the voltage at the pad and the voltage at the connector are not the same
number. Use a pin whose divider ratio you have verified, or verify it as part
of this experiment.
:::

### 1. Identify the board {#sec-s1-step-identify}

```bash
arduino-io list
arduino-io info
```

Write down, into the sidecar, four things from `info`: the board model, the
ADC resolution (`adc_bits`), the reference voltage (`vref_mV`), and whether
the `flags` line contains `streaming`. Everything downstream depends on them,
and `adc_bits` in particular is what the board *reports* — S1 will tell you
how many of those bits carry information.

If `streaming` is missing, the board is a Renesas one or carries firmware
older than the streaming support. The static half of this experiment still
works with `arduino-io monitor`; the timestamp analysis of
@sec-s1-step-noise does not, and needs one of the boards listed on this
experiment's overview page.

### 2. Wire the reference {#sec-s1-step-wire}

You need three input voltages and a way to know each of them better than the
board does. A tier-1 bench gives exactly that:

1. **0 V** — the input pin shorted to GND.
2. **$V_\mathrm{ref}/2$** — the reference IC through a two-resistor divider.
3. **$V_\mathrm{ref,IC}$** — the reference IC directly.

Build the divider from two resistors of the same nominal value; its exact
ratio does not matter, because you are going to measure the voltage it
produces rather than compute it.

::: {.callout-important}
## Measure at the pin, not at the source

Put the DMM probes on the pin and the ground closest to it, with the board
powered and the wiring exactly as it will be during the acquisition. A
contact resistance, a shared ground return or a divider loaded by the input
impedance all show up here and nowhere else. Record the DMM reading and its
uncertainty (from the instrument's specification, for the range you used) in
`channels[].reference_value` and `channels[].reference_u`.
:::

### 3. The three calibration points {#sec-s1-step-cal}

Put the pin in analog mode once, then take one recording per point. Two
hundred records at 1 kHz is a fifth of a second and is plenty:

```bash
arduino-io mode 15 analog
arduino-io stream 15 --hz 1000 --seconds 0.2 --csv data/cal-0v.csv
```

Between points, change the wiring, **re-measure with the DMM**, and write a
new sidecar. Do not reuse a DMM reading from ten minutes ago: the reference IC
warms up, and so does the room.

Name the files after the point (`cal-0v`, `cal-1v25`, `cal-2v50`), so the
analysis can find them without a lookup table.

### 4. The noise and timing run {#sec-s1-step-noise}

Leave the reference on the first pin, short a second pin to GND, and record
both together for five seconds:

```bash
arduino-io mode 15 analog && arduino-io mode 16 analog
arduino-io stream 15,16 --hz 1000 --seconds 5 --csv data/noise-linux.csv
```

The shorted channel is not a formality. It shows the noise floor of the
converter and the board's own ground with no contribution from the source, so
comparing the two channels separates "the reference is noisy" from "the
converter is noisy".

Copy the whole summary line into `stream_stats`. All six counters at zero
means a complete recording; anything else has to be either explained or
re-acquired, and the analysis template will say so.

### 5. The same acquisition on a second host {#sec-s1-step-host}

Move the board — the same board, the same firmware, the same cable — to a
host running a different operating system, and repeat @sec-s1-step-noise
exactly:

```bash
arduino-io stream 15,16 --hz 1000 --seconds 5 --csv data/noise-macos.csv
```

Nothing about the measurand changed. Whatever differs between the two files is
the host, and quantifying that difference is the point of this step.

::: {.callout-tip}
## If you only have one host

Approximate it: run the second acquisition while the host is busy — a large
file copy, or a build — and record what you did in `environment.notes`. The
comparison is then between an idle and a loaded host rather than between two
operating systems, which demonstrates the same mechanism and is honest as long
as you say so.
:::

### 6. Fill the sidecars {#sec-s1-step-sidecar}

Before you leave the bench, every one of the five runs needs its sidecar
complete. The fields nobody can reconstruct afterwards:

- [ ] `board.adc_bits`, `board.vref_mV`, `board.usbio_version` — from `arduino-io info`
- [ ] `host.os`, `host.machine`, `host.hub` — including whether a USB hub was in the path
- [ ] `acquisition.requested_period_us` **and** `acquisition.achieved_rate_hz`
- [ ] all six `stream_stats` counters, from the summary line
- [ ] per channel: `reference_value` and `reference_u`, from the DMM at the pin
- [ ] `references[]`: the DMM model and its calibration state
- [ ] `synthetic: false`
